topics.title: Employment: people, participation and measurement
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate the labour force, workers and unemployed before interpreting a rate. This pilot covers selected concepts, not the entire unemployment chapter.

nodes.label: Employment measurement
Labour force: employed plus unemployed
LFPR: labour force / population
Workforce: those actually employed
Unemployment rate: unemployed / labour force
Underemployment: work below skill or education level (notes' example)

tables.title: Know the numerator and denominator

cells: LFPR
Labour force
Population of the defined group
Do not switch age group or reference period in a comparison.
Workforce participation rate
Employed people
Population of the defined group
Employment is not the same as labour-force membership.
Unemployment rate
Unemployed people
Labour force of the defined group
The denominator is not the entire population.

tables.title: Diagnose the employment constraint before choosing a policy

cells: Seasonal
Work disappears in predictable parts of a production calendar.
Consider off-season livelihood diversification, not only vacancy information.
Disguised
Removing a redundant worker need not reduce output.
Enable productive non-farm work; counting everyone as working can hide low productivity.
Structural
Skills, geography or the production structure do not match labour demand.
Match training and mobility support to actual vacancies; demand support alone may not resolve mismatch.
Frictional
Temporary search and movement between jobs.
Improve information and matching rather than classify every search spell as a permanent skills deficit.
Cyclical
Economy-wide weakness reduces demand for workers.
Diagnose the demand downturn; distinguish it from predictable seasonality.

tables.title: ILO: employment quality beyond headcounts (static background, not a new event)

cells: ILO's work-related mandate
Employment opportunities, rights, social protection and dialogue offer separate dimensions for a jobs answer.
An employment-rate observation does not measure every aspect of decent work.
Standards versus outcomes
Distinguish international standards, domestic implementation and actual worker conditions.
The notes do not prove that every standard applies as enforceable Indian law.

tables.title: Report evidence: framework, India application and verification

cells: Government of India / Economic Survey 2025-26 (claimed)
The jobs discussion combines employment estimates, organised-manufacturing employment, portal registrations and vacancies. These measure different populations and events.
Separate employed persons from registered workers, advertised vacancies and training places before evaluating job creation; retain age coverage and reference quarter.

Portal registration or a vacancy is not a realised job. Labour-code recognition is not proof that benefits have reached every eligible worker. Supplied secondary compilation only; official edition and underlying evidence have not been verified.
World Bank / WDR 2026 (claimed AI theme)
The selected page prioritises foundational skills and warns that tax incentives favouring automation over hiring can affect labour demand.
Illustrative application: evaluate an AI subsidy by worker productivity, displacement, reskilling and access for small firms, not adoption alone.
This is a policy mechanism, not an India employment forecast. The claimed WDR theme and edition require official confirmation.

tables.title: Scheme design: beneficiaries, delivery and source-era limits

cells: MGNREGS / MGNREGA
Rural Development; demand-based rural livelihood security through unskilled manual work.
Rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work; the guarantee unit is the household, not each adult separately.
Job-card and work-demand route through local government; the source describes time-bound work provision, unemployment allowance and Gram Sabha social audit.
Source separates Central financing of unskilled wages from shared material/skilled costs; this is public wage employment, not an insurance premium.

Work demand → employment/income support → potential community assets. Delayed provision/payment or weak social audit can weaken protection. Do not use the note's wage-law sentence as a current legal rule. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.
e-Shram portal
Labour and Employment; national database of unorganised workers and support for welfare-scheme delivery.
Source explicitly includes migrant, construction, gig and platform workers; it does not supply a complete enrolment eligibility/exclusion rule.
Records identity, occupation, address, education, skills and family details to support employability and welfare delivery.
Administrative database/delivery infrastructure; no automatic cash benefit or funding split is specified on this page.

Identification can reduce fragmentation, but registration is not itself proof that a worker qualifies for every linked social-security scheme. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: population 1,000; labour force 600; employed 540. Find LFPR and unemployment rate.
cards.answer: LFPR = 600/1,000 = 60%. Unemployed = 600 - 540 = 60; unemployment rate = 60/600 = 10%. The numbers are invented for practice, not observed labour statistics.

cards.question: Are everyone in the labour force and everyone employed the same set?
cards.answer: No. Labour force includes employed and unemployed people; workforce refers to the employed.

cards.question: Illustrative case: labour force falls from 500 to 450 while employed stays 400. Does falling unemployment prove more jobs?
cards.answer: Initially UR = (500 - 400)/500 = 20%; later UR = (450 - 400)/450 ≈ 11.1%. No new job appears. Participation has fallen, so read LFPR and WPR alongside UR. The invented example holds the underlying population constant.

cards.question: Illustrative case: six farm workers produce the same output as four. Is that the same as having no work after harvest?
cards.answer: No. The first is a stylised disguised-unemployment case: some labour is redundant. The second is seasonal unemployment. Their causes and remedies differ even if both reflect underused labour.

cards.question: Why should rates not be compared without their reference-period definitions?
cards.answer: A usual-status lens and a weekly or daily lens can capture different work patterns. The notes' exact classification wording contains inconsistencies, so use this distinction conceptually and verify official PLFS rules before quoting thresholds.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Employment-centred growth requires more than a low unemployment rate.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define labour force/workforce and rate denominators → contrast participation with unemployment → diagnose seasonal, disguised, structural or cyclical constraints → match job creation, skills and matching policies to causes → discuss work quality and underemployment → evaluate with multiple indicators and consistent reference periods.

cards.question: What is the expanded depth goal for this existing employment packet?
cards.answer: Retain the original measurement map; add denominator fluency, unemployment diagnosis and mechanism-led policy evaluation. Practise a rate case and a balanced descriptive plan. Do not memorise erroneous UPS/UPSS wording, assume a lower UR always means more work, or rely on unverified law-replacement claims.

cards.question: Illustrative case: vacancies require technical skills, while applicants lack them. Why might a general spending boost be insufficient?
cards.answer: The stated constraint is structural mismatch. A defensible response links demand for specific skills to training and access to suitable jobs; merely expanding spending does not guarantee applicants can fill those positions.

cards.question: Illustrative prompt: employment rises, but protection and working conditions remain weak. How would you deepen the answer?
cards.answer: Keep the employment measure, then evaluate rights, security and social dialogue separately. Name a mechanism and implementation constraint instead of treating a higher headcount as sufficient. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Recall: why should e-Shram registrations, vacancies and employment counts not be added together?
cards.answer: They count different things, can overlap and use different periods or populations. Registration indicates administrative reach; employment requires a defined labour-market measure.

cards.question: Answer framework: can AI adoption generate inclusive employment in India?
cards.answer: Original planning prompt: define productivity versus displacement; examine foundational skills, firm information and finance gaps; assess tax incentives and worker transitions; conclude with productivity and job-quality indicators. Treat the compilation's policy discussion as unverified, not an observed outcome.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: two adult members of one rural household volunteer for work. Does the source promise a separate annual guarantee to each?
cards.answer: No: the described guarantee is 100 days per rural household per financial year, not 100 per adult. Household-level protection differs from counting individual workers employed. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Trace the employment-guarantee mechanism and identify an implementation bottleneck.
cards.answer: Documented demand should trigger time-bound employment; failure is linked in the note to unemployment allowance. Gram Sabha social audit provides accountability. Demand not recorded or delayed provision can break the protection chain. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: a migrant platform worker registers on e-Shram and assumes every welfare payment is now assured. What is the error?
cards.answer: The database explicitly includes such worker categories, but registration supports identification/delivery; it does not prove eligibility for every underlying benefit. The cited page supplies no universal payment promise. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

facts.label: MGNREGA household guarantee and response period in supplied notes

observations.value: 100 days per financial year per rural household volunteering adult labour; employment within 15 days of demand, failing which the note describes unemployment allowance. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

updates.title: Employment: keep the denominator and job quality visible
updates.body: The women-in-agriculture item is a useful labour-measurement case, not a new confirmed employment rate. Distinguish female workers in agriculture as a share of all female workers from women as a share of the entire agricultural workforce. Do not copy the compilation's numeric claim until the denominator, period and original table are confirmed. The date denotes the compilation edition, not a verified event/effective date. Verify the official release before memorising details.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: The labour force contains employed people and unemployed people who meet the survey's job-search and availability criteria. The workforce contains employed people only. People outside the labour force are not automatically unemployed: they may be studying, performing unpaid household duties or not seeking/available for work under the relevant definition.

LFPR = labour force / population of the specified group x 100. WPR = employed / population of that same group x 100. Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force x 100. All three require an age group, reference period and activity-status definition. Without those, a percentage is incomplete.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Employment and unemployment change through both job outcomes and participation. Someone finding work moves from unemployed to employed. Someone stopping job search may move out of the labour force. Both can reduce measured unemployment, but their economic meaning is very different.

Employment quality matters beyond the employed/not-employed distinction. Hours, productivity, earnings, security and access to protection affect livelihoods. Seasonal unemployment concerns work availability at different times of year; disguised underemployment concerns workers whose removal would not materially reduce output in the stylised example. Structural mismatch differs from a cyclical fall in demand.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented group: population 1,000, labour force 600, employed 540. Unemployed people number 60. LFPR is 60%, WPR is 54%, and unemployment is 60 / 600 x 100 = 10%. Dividing the unemployed by total population would produce 6%, which is not the unemployment rate.

Now suppose 20 unemployed people stop searching and leave the labour force; employment remains 540. The labour force becomes 580 and unemployment becomes 40 / 580 = 6.90%. The unemployment rate fell without a single new job. Read LFPR and WPR together before calling this an improvement in labour demand.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A lower unemployment rate is not unconditionally good news. Higher LFPR may initially raise measured unemployment if new entrants seek jobs faster than employers create them. Neither a survey headline nor registration on a jobs portal proves all workers have secure, adequately paid work.
Do not mix usual-status and short-reference-period estimates, rural and urban groups, or different ages. A comparison can be numerically correct but economically invalid if its populations differ.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For an employment answer, separate labour supply, job creation and job quality. Connect skills and care constraints to participation, investment and demand to opportunities, and worker protection to quality. Use a matched LFPR/WPR/unemployment set, then explain the policy trade-off rather than inferring success from one rate.

topics.title: Motivation: diagnose the broken link
topics.subject: Management
topics.summary: Compare what motivates an employee with how motivation works. Apply theory to a case instead of memorising author names alone.

nodes.label: Motivation: needs and decision processes
Content theories ask what motivates
Process theories ask how motivation occurs
Herzberg: hygiene factors versus motivators
Vroom: expectancy, instrumentality, valence
Adams: perceived fairness of treatment

tables.title: Vroom: three distinct checks

cells: Expectancy
Can my effort produce the required performance?
Training, resources and feasible targets.
Instrumentality
Will performance actually produce the reward?
Credible, transparent performance-to-reward decisions.
Valence
Do I value this reward?
Discover what this employee values instead of assuming all want the same reward.

tables.title: Which theory fits the clue?

cells: Herzberg
Job conditions versus intrinsic achievement/growth
Removing a source of dissatisfaction is not identical to adding a motivator.
Vroom
A weak link between effort, performance and a valued outcome
Reward value alone does not establish a credible performance-to-reward link.
Adams
Perceived unfairness in organisational treatment
Fairness is a perception to investigate, not simply identical pay for everyone.

cards.question: Illustrative case: an employee wants promotion but thinks selection ignores performance. Diagnose the weak Vroom component.
cards.answer: Instrumentality: the employee does not believe performance will produce the desired reward. A credible selection process addresses this link; a larger reward alone may not.

cards.question: Change the case: selection is fair, but the employee doubts they can meet the target. What changed?
cards.answer: The weak link is expectancy: effort is not expected to yield the required performance. Consider ability, support and target feasibility.

teaching_notes.title: 10. Tokenisation and atomic settlement: faster exchange, not guaranteed value
paragraphs: Tokenisation represents a financial claim using a digital record. The bond remains an obligation of its issuer under its terms: changing the record-keeping technology does not by itself improve the issuer's cash flow or remove credit risk. The compilation describes a corporate-bond tokenisation pilot linked to wholesale digital rupee infrastructure.

Atomic settlement aims to make the security transfer and payment conditional on one another so that one side is not completed alone. Invented bond sale: buyer transfers Rs 10 lakh only as the corresponding bond is delivered. This addresses a settlement mismatch, not a fall in the bond's market value or failure of future interest payments.

Do not confuse wholesale CBDC used in settlement with every retail programmable-payment use case. A pilot is evidence of testing a mechanism, not universal market deployment or a finding that custody, operational, legal and cyber risks have all disappeared.

cards.question: Application: an energy-shock assumption changes after a forecast. Must the earlier forecast be called an observed error immediately?
cards.answer: No. First identify the original conditional baseline, forecast horizon and later information. Compare the revised forecast or realised outcome on the same definition; do not silently replace the vintage.

updates.title: October growth-forecast comparison
updates.body: The supplied compilation reports India forecasts from the World Bank and IMF. Keep the two publisher-specific fact records separate. Link growth mechanisms to ESI, while using labour data rather than GDP alone for employment conclusions. This pilot covers only one selected economic-current-affairs item.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: A growth forecast is a conditional estimate of future output growth, not an observed GDP result or a policy target. It depends on assumptions about demand, prices, trade, policy and shocks. Different institutions can reasonably publish different forecasts because their information, assumptions or methods differ.

A complete forecast entry needs the institution, report, release date or edition, economy, forecast period and fiscal/calendar basis. Without these, a bare number can mislead. India's financial year and a calendar year cover different months, so forecasts using those periods cannot be casually compared.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: A revision changes an institution's earlier forecast for the same horizon. A difference between two institutions is not necessarily a revision. The base also matters: a rebound from a weak previous year can produce high percentage growth without implying an equally large improvement over the pre-shock path.

Forecasts are useful for discussing risks and direction, but not proof that jobs, household income or poverty will improve equally. The link depends on sectoral composition, employment intensity, prices and distribution. Use appropriate labour or social evidence for those separate claims.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative table: institution A forecasts 7.1% and institution B 7.0% for the same stated year. The 0.1 percentage-point gap does not prove one is wrong. First check whether both measure real growth and use the same year, then examine release timing and assumptions.

If A previously forecast 6.8% and now forecasts 7.1%, the revision is +0.3 percentage points, not +0.3% growth in the forecast economy. The relative change in the forecast number is a different calculation and rarely the intended exam answer.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not confuse percentage points with percent, a target with a forecast, real with nominal growth or an edition date with the reference year. Retain the old forecast when recording a revision so its direction is visible.

The 7.1% and 7.0% values appearing in supplied compilations are source claims, not independently verified current forecasts. These explanations teach comparison without endorsing the figures as official.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Use a forecast as one dated piece of evidence: state who expects what for which period, explain the underlying risk and add a limitation. For recall, compare publisher and horizon together, then practise identifying a revised number without merging different institutions into one supposed series.

cards.question: Illustrative case: grain stocks rise but child nutrition remains weak. What distinction matters?
cards.answer: Availability is only the quantitative dimension. Examine diet quality, access and the delivery of nutritional support before concluding that food security has improved.

cards.question: Build a descriptive outline on agricultural market reform.
cards.answer: Define the marketing problem; explain information/competition barriers; discuss market-linking interventions; evaluate access, implementation and producer outcomes; conclude with safeguards. Do not list portals without mechanisms.

cards.question: Why can a farm-support measure have both benefits and costs?
cards.answer: Support can reduce risk or costs but alter resource use and distribution. Analyse the particular subsidy rather than asserting that all support is good or bad.

cards.question: What is enough depth for this sector packet?
cards.answer: Explain food security, market reform and one support trade-off closed-book, then practise a scheme eligibility case using current verified rules. Skip crop encyclopaedias and stale numeric limits; retain syllabus breadth.

cards.question: Outline an evaluation of a sustainable-input campaign.
cards.answer: State the resource problem; explain behaviour/incentive channels; assess extension reach and farmer constraints; identify outcome measures for soil, water and yields; discuss trade-offs rather than merely naming the campaign. This is an analytical practice prompt, not proof of the programme's measured impact.

cards.question: Connect agricultural productivity to food security without assuming the two are identical.
cards.answer: Trace production and supply, purchasing/access conditions, diet quality and food safety. Use household and nutritional evidence separately from agricultural output. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Answer framework: why is foodgrain output insufficient evidence of nutrition security?
cards.answer: Original outline: distinguish availability, access, affordability and dietary diversity; connect productivity and value chains to local food prices; add household resources and targeted protection; monitor nutritious-diet costs rather than only aggregate tonnage.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: a landholding family includes a member who paid income tax in the last assessment year. Does a small farm guarantee PM-KISAN eligibility?
cards.answer: No under the described source-era rule: family-level income-tax exclusion can override landholding eligibility. Do not test only farm size. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: the only proposed exclusion is that a farmer is a Group D government employee. Automatically reject the family?
cards.answer: No: the cited employee exclusion expressly excepts MTS/Class IV/Group D. Check all other family-level conditions; the exception alone is not a guarantee of eligibility. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: husband and wife both own cultivable plots and have minor children. Two PM-KISAN family entitlements?
cards.answer: Not under the cited family definition: husband, wife and minor children form one family; multiple land titles do not automatically create multiple family entitlements. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: an FPO plans a viable warehouse and asks whether AIF pays off the entire project loan.
cards.answer: No: AIF is debt financing with specified interest/guarantee support, not a universal principal waiver. The FPO remains a borrower and the project must fit eligible infrastructure. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

updates.title: Agriculture and sustainability: soil, water and input use
updates.body: The compilation describes a planned Khet Bachao Abhiyan - Rabi 2026 campaign, with soil health, balanced input use, natural/regenerative practices and water conservation. Use it as a static-policy connection: input choice -> soil/water effects -> farm resilience. A programme announcement does not establish implementation or effectiveness. The date denotes the compilation edition, not a verified event/effective date. Verify the official release before memorising details.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Agriculture supports food supply, rural livelihoods and inputs for other sectors. Agricultural development is therefore more than maximising one crop's output: productivity, farm income, risk, resource use and access to food must be considered together. A rise in production can coexist with weak earnings if costs rise or realised prices fall.

Food security includes availability, access, utilisation and stability. Grain stocks concern availability; purchasing power and delivery concern access; nutrition, health and diet quality affect utilisation. A country can have adequate aggregate food and still have households unable to obtain a nutritious diet.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Productivity depends on technology, water, soil, knowledge and reliable inputs. Marketing determines how output becomes income: information, transport, storage and competition affect realised prices. Electronic market links can improve information and reach, but cannot alone remove physical logistics or bargaining constraints.

Support policies alter incentives. Cheap power can lower irrigation costs while encouraging excessive groundwater use if extraction is not managed. Price support can reduce some price risk while concentrating gains in crops or regions with stronger procurement access. Assess distribution and ecological effects alongside the intended support.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative farmer harvests more vegetables, but poor storage forces immediate sale when local supply is abundant. Output rose while the realised price fell. Storage, logistics, market information and access to buyers address a different constraint from raising yield.

A district has abundant grain yet persistent child malnutrition. Investigate dietary diversity, household access, sanitation, illness and the reliability of nutrition delivery. More grain production alone need not solve every pathway to poor nutrition.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate production, productivity and farm income. A portal registration is not proof of competitive price discovery. A support price announcement is not proof that all farmers sell at that price.

A food subsidy, farm loan, insurance product and market reform solve different problems. Scheme-era amounts and beneficiary rules require current verification; examples here explain mechanisms rather than endorse operative eligibility.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For agricultural reform, begin with the constraint: productivity, price risk, market access, credit or sustainability. Explain the instrument's channel, then uneven access and implementation. Conclude with income resilience and nutrition/resource outcomes rather than a target or portal count alone.

cards.question: Illustrative case: approvals become easier but a plant is not built. Is reform necessarily ineffective?
cards.answer: Separate the intended reduction in permission friction from investment outcomes. Identify other constraints and evaluate actual investment, productivity and jobs rather than portal activity alone.

cards.question: Compare delicensing and disinvestment.
cards.answer: Delicensing concerns entry/expansion permission; disinvestment concerns government equity. They are distinct reform instruments with different transmission channels.

cards.question: Plan a 400-word answer on industrial reform.
cards.answer: Define the constraint; select reform instruments; trace incentives into investment/productivity; assess implementation and inclusion; conclude. Use a few verified current anchors, not every historical policy date.

cards.question: Depth checkpoint: what should be retrieved?
cards.answer: Explain two reform mechanisms and two distinct approval/site-information tools. Add a limitation to each. Current institutional counts in the notes are not permanent facts.

cards.question: Which indicators would test whether a single-window reform works?
cards.answer: Approval time and predictability are intermediate measures; investment implementation and productive outcomes are separate checks. Establish the baseline, metric definition and period before comparing numbers. This is an analytical practice prompt, not proof of the programme's measured impact.

cards.question: Outline an industrial-growth answer using inclusive and sustainable criteria.
cards.answer: Explain productive capacity and competitiveness; test who gains jobs/income; examine resource and pollution effects; propose implementation safeguards. Do not use the acronym as a substitute for causal reasoning. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Illustrative ESI prompt: why can an insolvency framework matter beyond bank recovery?
cards.answer: Explain coordination, the preservation/reallocation of productive assets and orderly exit. Then discuss delay and implementation capacity. Do not assume the source's amendment proposals are in force; exact legal rules need verification.

updates.title: Industry: approval activity versus investment outcomes
updates.body: The compilation reports an expanded National Single Window System and lists application/approval/service counts. The static industry notes explain the platform's guidance and application role. Do not compare unlike counts (services, approvals, ministries and states) as one measure. Administrative throughput is not automatically productive investment or employment. The date denotes the compilation edition, not a verified event/effective date. Verify the official release before memorising details.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Industrial development expands productive capacity and can support employment, technology and linkages with suppliers. Its contribution depends not only on factory output but also on productivity, working conditions, competitive capability and the ability of smaller firms to participate.

Delicensing reduces specified prior permissions for entry or expansion. Disinvestment changes the government's equity holding. Privatisation involves a transfer into private ownership/control. These instruments address different decisions, so they cannot be used as synonyms.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Firms invest when expected returns justify costs and risks. Simpler approvals can reduce delays, but infrastructure, skills, finance, land access and demand still affect whether investment happens. An information or application portal is a coordination tool, not proof that every approval has been legally granted.

Industrial policy can address coordination failures, technology gaps and infrastructure. It can also create fiscal costs and distort competition if support is poorly targeted or indefinitely protected. Evaluate whether support builds capabilities and whether firms face incentives to become productive rather than depend permanently on assistance.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative plant receives clearer information about approvals, yet construction stalls because power supply is unreliable and logistics are costly. The approval reform may have reduced one friction without making the whole project viable. Diagnose the remaining bottleneck instead of calling every reform either a complete success or a failure.

If government sells a small shareholding while retaining control, that is disinvestment but not necessarily privatisation. If licensing requirements are reduced, ownership may remain unchanged. The relevant transmission channels are incentives, control and entry barriers, not the labels alone.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A memorandum of understanding, announced investment, sanctioned project and operating plant are different stages. Production growth is not automatically broad job creation if the activity is highly capital-intensive.
Delicensing is not exemption from labour, environmental, competition or other applicable laws. A single-window interface does not mean every legal authority and safeguard has disappeared.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Build an industrial-policy answer around the bottleneck, the chosen instrument and the intended productivity or employment channel. Add infrastructure, skills and competition conditions, then evaluate realised output, supplier linkages and jobs. Separate announcements and approvals from implementation and outcomes.

topics.title: Services: output, jobs, insurance and logistics
topics.subject: ESI

nodes.label: Services: output, jobs, insurance and logistics
GDP share, employment and productivity are different indicators

Insurance density: premiums per person
Logistics policy: coordination and cost competitiveness

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: Output share
Measures a sector's contribution to output.
A large output share does not by itself establish an equally large employment share.
Labour productivity
Output per unit of labour input.
Specify persons or hours and compare like periods.
Insurance penetration versus density
Premium/GDP versus premium/population.
The denominators and units differ; neither alone measures claim quality or protection adequacy.
Logistics policy
Aims to improve costs, coordination and data-driven decisions.
Targets are not achieved outcomes.

cards.question: Original practice: premiums are 40 units, GDP is 1,000 units and population is 20. Calculate penetration and density.
cards.answer: Penetration = 40/1,000 x 100 = 4%. Density = 40/20 = 2 currency units per person. These inputs are invented to test the denominators.

cards.question: Does fast services growth guarantee enough jobs for all skill groups?
cards.answer: No. Compare employment with output and examine skill requirements/productivity. The two shares cannot be substituted for each other.

cards.question: Build a services-led development answer outline.
cards.answer: Describe output/jobs/export channels; distinguish subsectors; explain productivity and access constraints; evaluate logistics/digital support; conclude on broad employment quality. Do not treat all services as equally skill-intensive.

cards.question: How much sector trivia should be retained?
cards.answer: Learn the indicator distinctions and two subsector mechanisms deeply. Use dated verified numbers only when they support an argument; do not memorise every projected market size.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Services include a wide range of activities, from trade and transport to healthcare, finance and professional work. They differ greatly in skill requirements and productivity. A large services share of GDP therefore does not imply that every worker can immediately obtain a well-paid service job.

Output share measures contribution to production; employment share measures where people work. Labour productivity relates output to workers or hours. A sector can produce a high share of output with fewer workers, while many people remain in lower-productivity activities.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Services can support other sectors: logistics connects producers to markets, finance mobilises resources, and communication reduces coordination costs. Weak services can raise costs throughout the economy. Development requires the supporting infrastructure and skills, not merely a new platform or headline growth rate.

Insurance penetration is premiums relative to GDP; insurance density is premiums per person. They measure different denominators. Neither directly measures adequate coverage, claim settlement or financial protection for vulnerable households. Increased premium payments can coexist with gaps in usable protection.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented premiums 40, GDP 1,000 and population 20 give penetration of 4% and density of 2 currency units per person. Density is not a percentage. These are mathematical illustrations, not actual insurance indicators.

A highly productive digital service expands output but recruits only specialised workers. Its growth may be valuable without absorbing all displaced low-skill workers. Skill development and a broader range of labour-absorbing activities are needed to connect output growth with inclusive employment.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate a high output share with an equal employment share or use penetration and density interchangeably. Insurance sales are not proof that customers understand exclusions or can obtain adequate claims.
A logistics target is not an achieved cost reduction. Compare consistent coverage, units and reference periods before repeating a claim about India's service or insurance performance.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Explain the service's direct contribution and its linkages with other sectors. Distinguish high-productivity segments from broad employment opportunities, then address skills and access. For insurance, combine reach with product suitability, affordability and protection rather than treating premium volume as the whole objective.

cards.question: Illustrative classification: buying goods abroad versus buying a foreign financial asset.
cards.answer: The goods purchase is a current-transaction example; the financial-asset purchase involves a capital/financial transaction. Applicable permissions still need checking.

cards.question: Can a services surplus matter even if merchandise trade is in deficit?
cards.answer: Yes. The notes explain that invisibles/services earnings and remittances can offset some goods-trade deficit. Inspect the complete accounts instead of equating the merchandise balance with the entire BoP.

cards.question: Outline an answer on opening the external sector.
cards.answer: Define the opening; explain trade and capital-flow channels; discuss competitiveness and financing; evaluate vulnerability and policy safeguards; conclude with a balanced judgement. Omit unsupported claims that all trade deficits are bad.

cards.question: Which source ambiguity needs resolving first?
cards.answer: Page 6 says current-account convertibility since 1994; page 19 states an August 1993 date. These are incompatible source observations of the stated milestone, not two confirmed historical facts.

cards.question: How would you avoid confusing an FTA, a financial safety net and a negotiating bloc?
cards.answer: Compare objective, instrument and obligations on common dimensions. Do not assume deeper integration, a common currency or a loan entitlement merely from membership. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Application: does a rise in announced greenfield project value prove an equal increase in realised FDI?
cards.answer: No. Project announcements, financing and realised investment differ in timing and coverage. Evaluate completion, financing conditions and sectoral allocation before inferring development benefits.

facts.label: Year of India's current-account convertibility milestone (source inconsistency)

observations.as_of: Undated notes, PDF page 6; historical milestone claim
Undated notes, PDF page 19; historical milestone claim

updates.title: Forex windows and swap rollovers
updates.body: A dedicated dollar-supply arrangement is not a grant or fixed exchange rate; extension of an existing drawdown is not necessarily a new facility. Source: supplied October compilation; not independently verified. The month denotes the edition, not proof of an event or effective date.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: The balance of payments records transactions between residents and the rest of the world during a period. Merchandise trade is only one part. Services, income, transfers and financial transactions also matter. A trade deficit is therefore not automatically a current-account deficit or a complete description of external financing.

The current account covers goods, services, primary income and secondary income/transfers. In formal BoP terminology, the capital account is narrower than the broad everyday phrase 'capital flows'; investment and borrowing flows are largely recorded in the financial account. Use the classification specified in the question.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: An economy with a current-account deficit must obtain corresponding financing or use reserves, with accounting conventions and other entries taken into account. A country can have a merchandise deficit partly offset by service exports and remittances. Financing composition influences risk: durable investment differs from flows that can reverse quickly.

FDI is associated with a lasting investment relationship, whereas portfolio flows concern securities without the same direct-investment relationship. Convertibility concerns exchanging currency for permitted transactions. Current-account convertibility does not imply unrestricted movement for all investment, borrowing or asset purchases.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented external accounts: goods balance -100, services +60, net primary income -10 and net secondary transfers +30. The current-account balance is -20, not -100. This simplified example shows why merchandise balance cannot stand in for the whole current account.

Importing a machine is a goods transaction even though the machine is an investment asset for its buyer. Purchasing a foreign security is a financial transaction. The economic use of an item and its external-account classification are related but not identical questions.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: BoP balances as an accounting system; the phrase 'BoP deficit' usually refers to a particular analytical balance or financing pressure, not an assertion that the full accounting record cannot balance. Check sign conventions before interpreting reserve changes.

The supplied notes give conflicting current-account-convertibility years. No year is selected here as verified. Never infer legal permission, ownership thresholds or a current foreign-exchange rule from a simplified label alone.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For external vulnerability, discuss the current-account need, the stability and cost of financing, reserve/liquidity buffers and currency or maturity mismatches. Distinguish global price shocks from exchange-rate effects. Explain why the composition of transactions matters before quoting a headline deficit.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Foreign-exchange support, swaps and derivative risk
paragraphs: Oil importers need foreign currency to pay overseas suppliers. The compilation describes a special dollar-supply window for named public-sector oil companies. Routing some demand through a central-bank facility can change pressure in the open market. It is not free foreign currency, a cancellation of the import bill or a guarantee of a fixed exchange rate.

A currency-swap facility is the arrangement under which access is possible; a drawdown is the amount actually used; rollover extends the existing funding under agreed terms. The Maldives item describes a Rs 3,000 crore drawdown extension. A rollover is not automatically a fresh grant of the same size, and a facility ceiling is not necessarily the amount outstanding.

A non-deliverable derivative settles a difference in value rather than exchanging the full principal currencies. Hedging offsets an underlying risk; speculation takes exposure to an anticipated movement. Notional principal is a reference amount, not the current loss or cash exchanged. The compilation's new NDDC restrictions and 20% FERR are held as unverified rule claims; do not extend them to every forex contract or infer actual capital from notional value.

cards.question: Which two institutions are jointly called the World Bank?
cards.answer: IBRD and IDA. The World Bank Group is broader; distinguish IFC and the other arms rather than treating every name as interchangeable.

cards.question: Which report fields should be retrieved beyond a publisher name?
cards.answer: Publisher, edition/reference period, framework/measure, findings and India implications. The notes identify World Bank reports such as World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects; the monthly forecast packet supplies a dated illustration.

cards.question: Build a comparison-based globalisation answer.
cards.answer: Choose a function or problem first, then compare institutional mandates, financing/rules and practical limitations. Avoid a disconnected list of headquarters and presidents.

cards.question: What should be updated rather than learned as permanent?
cards.answer: Membership, quota shares, leadership, eligibility thresholds and latest report findings. Keep the stable mandate map; verify mutable values against official releases.

cards.question: A question asks which institution fits infrastructure finance versus external liquidity pressure. What distinction should you make?
cards.answer: Match the financing need and instrument to the mandate. NDB/AIIB development finance, the CRA support mechanism and a negotiating group have different functions; current access conditions need separate verification. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Recall: which analytical question is the supplied WIR framework best suited to?
cards.answer: Cross-border investment flows, multinational enterprises and investment-policy choices. It is not a household nutrition survey or a comprehensive macro forecast; the supplied 2026 edition remains unverified.

updates.title: IMF / World Bank: connect mandates to dated report reading
updates.body: The October Spotlight compilation reports IMF and World Bank growth projections. Use the existing Growth forecasts topic to compare publisher, report, forecast horizon and revision date. Different publishers' projections are not two competing observations of one actual GDP outcome. Neither reported forecast has been independently verified here.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: International institutions solve different coordination and financing problems. The IMF is associated with international monetary cooperation and balance-of-payments support; development banks provide development finance; WTO provides an institutional framework for trade rules. Their mandates are not interchangeable merely because all work internationally.

The World Bank refers to IBRD and IDA together. The wider World Bank Group also includes other institutions, such as IFC, with distinct roles. IBRD development lending, IDA concessional support and IFC's private-sector orientation should not be assigned indiscriminately to a single arm.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: IMF governance uses quotas and voting arrangements rather than a simple assumption of equal votes for each country on every decision. Institutional design affects resources, representation and policy conditions. Discuss both the purpose of assistance and the capacity to implement an adjustment or development programme.

Reports are another institutional output. To use one intelligently, identify publisher, edition, reference period, subject measured, methodology and a relevant finding. WEO, a development report and an investment report do not measure the same thing. A forecast is conditional, a ranking relative and a historical observation tied to its period.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative request to fund a long-term public-health infrastructure project suggests a development-finance problem. A temporary external-payments financing gap suggests a different need. Match the financing purpose and terms before selecting the institution rather than using 'international loan' as the only clue.

If two reports give different growth forecasts, first compare institution, release date and fiscal/calendar basis. Their difference does not by itself reveal an error. If a ranking falls while a score improves, other countries may have improved faster; rank and level are distinct.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: World Bank and World Bank Group are not identical; WTO and GATT are not simply two current names for an unchanged institution. The presence of 'UN' or a regional grouping name does not make every associated body a lender or regulator.

A compilation's publisher attribution or latest-edition label can be wrong. Treat supplied report figures as unverified until authenticated; do not invent report release dates or equate edition with the data year.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For objective preparation, learn institution -> mandate -> instrument -> report, adding a confusable neighbour. For a descriptive answer, evaluate financing, coordination and implementation with country capacity and representation. Use report findings as evidence supporting an argument, not as a substitute for explaining the argument.

topics.title: Economic thought: assumptions, demand and policy response
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective theory support: compare classical adjustment and Keynesian demand management intuitively. Do not let advanced diagrams displace higher-priority ESI issues.

nodes.label: Economic thought: assumptions, demand and policy response
Classical presentation: flexible wages/prices and long-run adjustment
Keynesian presentation: short-run constraints
Insufficient demand can restrain output and employment
Public spending can support demand in a depressed economy

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: Time horizon
Classical discussion stresses long-run adjustment; Keynesian discussion stresses short-run conditions.
Do not compare conclusions without comparing assumptions.
Wage/price adjustment
Flexibility supports a self-adjusting account.
Rigidities change the speed and outcome of adjustment.
Demand shortfall
Spending can restrain output when productive capacity is unused.
Do not assume the same response when capacity and supply are binding.
Government role
Laissez-faire versus active demand support in the stylised comparison.
These are learning models, not universal policy slogans.

cards.question: Illustrative case: unused capacity and falling demand. What channel could public expenditure support?
cards.answer: Aggregate spending can support output and employment when demand is deficient. State the unused-capacity assumption and discuss limits; do not promise a costless outcome.

cards.question: Why are model assumptions examinable?
cards.answer: Changing the time horizon, adjustment speed or capacity assumptions can change the conclusion. Explain the mechanism instead of memorising that one school is always correct.

cards.question: Stopping rule for this chapter?
cards.answer: Retrieve the common comparison dimensions and apply one demand-shock case. Return to this reference only when a policy question reveals a gap; advanced derivations are lower priority.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Economic schools are sets of assumptions and explanations, not slogans that one side always favours government and another always opposes it. A useful comparison asks about the time horizon, adjustment of wages/prices, unused capacity and what determines output and employment.

A stylised classical account emphasises long-run adjustment and the role of flexible prices in coordinating resources. A Keynesian account highlights short-run situations in which weak aggregate demand and rigidities can leave resources unemployed. Changing these assumptions can change the policy conclusion.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: If firms lack orders, they may reduce output and employment despite available machinery and workers. A spending increase can support demand and activate idle capacity. Its size depends on leakages, imports, taxes, expectations and financial conditions; the presence of a demand channel is not a guarantee of a fixed multiplier.

When the economy is near capacity, extra demand may create more price pressure than real production. Supply-side improvements instead aim to increase productive capacity and efficiency. Demand support and supply reform are not mutually exclusive; they address different constraints over different horizons.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative factory can produce 100 units but sells only 60 and therefore employs fewer workers. Additional orders may raise output without a new plant because spare capacity exists. The key assumption is unmet demand for the factory's output, not merely that government has spent money somewhere.

If the same factory already operates at its practical capacity, extra orders can lead to higher prices, imports or delivery delays unless capacity expands. The same spending measure can therefore have different effects under different initial conditions.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not claim public spending always creates equivalent output or that flexible prices guarantee instant adjustment in every real economy. A model's prediction is conditional on its assumptions.

Distinguish a positive claim about how the economy behaves from a normative judgement about a desirable outcome. Historical schools and today's policy institutions do not map one-to-one onto simple labels.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Compare schools through assumptions -> mechanism -> predicted outcome -> policy implication. In an applied question, diagnose whether demand, capacity or allocation is the binding constraint. A conditional explanation is stronger than declaring one school universally right.

topics.title: Planning: objectives, instruments and institutional transition
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective historical breadth: remember the purpose and broad strategy shifts. Use the readable short notes; the full planning PDF has no extractable text and is catalogued as reference only.

nodes.label: Planning: objectives, instruments and institutional transition
Planning matches policy instruments to long-term objectives
Imperative versus indicative planning
Growth/jobs and distribution are distinct objectives
Planning Commission to NITI Aayog: institutional transition

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: Imperative planning
Directive allocation with a central authority.
Do not confuse it with all forms of government coordination.
Indicative planning
Government facilitates and influences private decisions.
A facilitator still shapes incentives and policy priorities.
Economic versus social objectives
Output/employment alongside distribution and justice.
A higher aggregate income does not automatically settle distribution.
Mahalanobis strategy
Emphasis on heavy/capital-goods industrial capacity and self-reliance.
The notes also describe foreign-exchange constraints: evaluate feasibility.

cards.question: Compare plan targets with outcomes: what is the basic trap?
cards.answer: A stated target is not an achieved outcome. Explain strategy and constraints rather than reproducing every target-growth table.

cards.question: Outline a short answer on planning institutions.
cards.answer: Explain planning purpose; distinguish planning types; trace broad institutional change; assess coordination and implementation. Treat plan-era budget classifications in old notes as historical, not automatically current.

cards.question: What should be prioritised over all twelve plan dates?
cards.answer: A few strategy transitions, growth-versus-distribution objectives, and the Commission-to-NITI transition. Use detailed chronology as reference for targeted gaps.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Economic planning coordinates objectives and resource use over time. It can aim at growth, employment, distribution and structural change when markets or institutions alone do not provide the desired coordination. Planning is not synonymous with government owning every enterprise.

Imperative planning relies on directives and central allocation. Indicative planning uses guidance, information, incentives and coordination while private decisions remain important. Both involve priorities; they differ in how decisions are made and implemented.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: The capital-goods emphasis associated with the Mahalanobis strategy sought to build the capacity to produce investment goods and reduce dependence. Its attraction was longer-term productive capability. Its constraints included the resources and foreign exchange needed now, the time before returns appeared and the need for agriculture and consumer supply.

Planning requires translating objectives into projects, finance and implementation. A target can fail through weak capacity, unrealistic assumptions, external shocks or poor monitoring. Institutional coordination and feedback matter even where detailed production targets have been replaced by more facilitative approaches.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative economy must choose between quickly expanding consumer output and devoting scarce resources to machinery that increases future production. The second option may build long-run capacity but creates near-term trade-offs. Neither choice can be judged without the objective, time horizon and constraints.

A plan sets 8% growth and achieves 6%. The target is an intention, the outcome a result. Explain investment, implementation or shock-related reasons before attributing the entire gap to the existence of planning itself.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate indicative planning with absence of state action or heavy-industry emphasis with ignoring every other sector. Avoid reproducing plan-era budget classifications as if they remain today's operative accounting.
Targets, allocations, expenditures and outcomes are distinct. Institutional transition does not mean the need for coordination, evaluation or long-term priorities disappears.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: An answer on planning should state the developmental problem, explain the chosen coordination instrument and analyse its constraints. Discuss agriculture-industry linkages and implementation rather than memorising only plan dates and target tables. Evaluate institutions by function, not merely their names.

topics.title: Before Independence: structural constraints and development
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective context for explaining reform needs: agricultural stagnation, structural dependence and the difference between demographic potential and realised development.

nodes.label: Before Independence: structural constraints and development
Agriculture: livelihood dependence with weak productivity
Cash-crop orientation and colonial trade incentives
Industrial deterioration constrained diversification
Demographic dividend is potential, not an automatic benefit

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: Livelihood dependence
A large agricultural dependence can coexist with poor productivity.
Dependence is not a measure of agricultural prosperity.
Cash crops
Production incentives can shift toward export-oriented crops.
Production volume alone does not establish household food access.
Diversification
Weak industrial opportunities limit structural transformation.
Do not infer modern sector shares from colonial observations.
Demographic dividend
A working-age structure creates economic potential.
Jobs and human capabilities are needed to realise the opportunity.

cards.question: How can colonial context support an answer without overwhelming it?
cards.answer: Use one relevant structural constraint to explain why an intervention was pursued, then analyse its mechanism and outcome. Avoid an entire historical narrative in a current-policy answer.

cards.question: Does a working-age population automatically create a dividend?
cards.answer: No. The notes define economic potential from age structure; an answer still needs employment and capability channels.

cards.question: What is enough preparation depth?
cards.answer: Explain two structural constraints and one reform motivation. Keep historical numerical series in reference unless explicitly demanded.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: The colonial economy provides the structural starting point for later development policy: dependence on low-productivity agriculture, restricted industrial opportunity and weak capabilities limited productive diversification. Historical context helps explain why independent India emphasised food security, infrastructure and industrial capacity.

A population dependent on farming is not necessarily agriculturally prosperous. Dependence describes livelihood concentration; productivity, land access, prices and risk determine earnings. Limited alternatives can keep people in low-productivity activity even when incomes are poor.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Commercialisation can shift cultivation toward cash crops and external markets. That can change income opportunities, but food access also depends on purchasing power and distribution. Growing a valuable export crop does not automatically protect a household from hunger when prices, harvests or access fail.

Transport and infrastructure can expand trade, but their developmental effects depend on what they connect and whose objectives they serve. Evaluate productive linkages and local opportunities rather than assuming every increase in trade necessarily improves local welfare.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative district moves land toward a cash crop. Export receipts rise, but a crop failure and high food prices leave small growers unable to buy sufficient food. The mechanism distinguishes production incentives and aggregate trade from household vulnerability.

A present-day agricultural policy answer may use this history in one sentence to explain inherited dependence and weak diversification. It should then turn to today's mechanism and evidence, not spend the answer retelling an entire historical period.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not infer current sector shares from colonial descriptions or treat every page in a history-labelled compilation as data for the same era. Separate a historical observation from a general analytical concept.

Avoid a monocausal explanation in which one factor accounts for every later outcome. Land institutions, productive capability, external incentives and public services interact. Numerical claims require a historical period and a reliable measure.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Use the sequence inherited constraint -> post-independence objective -> intervention -> continuing challenge. This makes history analytical rather than decorative. Explain why expanding productive alternatives and capabilities mattered, while keeping claims tied to the historical period under discussion.

topics.title: 1947-1991: compare sector strategies and their constraints
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: A compact comparison across the historical macro, agriculture, industry, services and external-sector folders. These selected pages are context, not an exhaustive historical synthesis.

nodes.label: 1947-1991: compare sector strategies and their constraints
Macro: planned development from structural underdevelopment
Agriculture: land reform and an input/credit package
Industry: capital-goods strategy and rural demand linkages
Services: productivity and employment need separate checks
External policy: import substitution and self-reliance

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: Macro strategy
Planning sought growth from a weak structural starting point.
Targets, actual outcomes and shocks must be distinguished.
Land reform and Green Revolution inputs
Tenure/ownership measures differ from technology, water and credit support.
Unequal access can distribute gains unevenly.
Heavy industry
Capital-goods capacity formed a strategic priority.
Agricultural/rural-income weakness can reduce industrial demand.
Services
High productivity is not identical to broad employment absorption.
This history-labelled source includes later structural observations; do not assume every page describes only 1947-91.
Import substitution
Protection aimed to reduce external dependence and build domestic capability.
Assess costs and competitiveness as well as the intended objective.

cards.question: Illustrative mechanism: a farm-output shock affects a factory. Explain.
cards.answer: Lower agricultural output can reduce rural incomes and demand for industrial goods, while agro-based industries can also face input shortages. Distinguish demand and input channels.

cards.question: Compare agricultural land reform with an input package.
cards.answer: Land reform addresses ownership/tenure/incentives; input packages address technology and production resources. They address different constraints and can interact.

cards.question: Build a 1991-transition answer without listing every policy date.
cards.answer: Start with inherited constraints; contrast pre-reform sector strategies with opening/competition; evaluate intended channels and distribution; conclude using relevant evidence rather than chronology.

cards.question: What is the stopping rule for historical sector notes?
cards.answer: Retrieve one intervention, one mechanism and one limitation per sector. Deepen historical detail only when an actual practice demand reveals a gap.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: The 1947-1991 policy setting combined a major public role, planning and a protected industrial strategy. The objective was structural transformation from a weak productive base. Evaluate agriculture, industry and trade together because shortages or weak demand in one sector can constrain the others.

Land reform addresses ownership, tenancy and incentives. An agricultural input package addresses technology, irrigation, seeds and finance. These interventions solve different problems; improving one does not automatically remove the other constraint.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Heavy industry can build capital-goods capacity and long-run self-reliance. Agriculture supplies food, raw materials and rural demand for manufactured goods. Weak agricultural productivity can therefore reduce industrial demand while creating food or input constraints.

Import substitution protects or supports domestic production to replace imports. It can build capability, but prolonged protection without competitive discipline can also raise costs and weaken efficiency. Assess the learning and capacity rationale alongside performance incentives and foreign-exchange limitations.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative crop failure reduces farm income. Rural households buy fewer manufactured goods, reducing factory demand. An agro-processing factory may simultaneously face raw-material shortages. These are separate demand and input-supply channels linking agriculture and industry.

A tenant gains secure rights but lacks irrigation and affordable inputs. Tenure reform can improve incentives, yet productivity still faces a resource constraint. Conversely, an input package may benefit those with better land and water access more strongly.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not treat every adverse outcome as proof that the original objective was meaningless, or every capacity gain as proof that protection had no cost. Examine alternatives and constraints.
The supplied sector-history material includes later structural observations. Keep the date of an observation separate from the chapter label. Targets and actual outcomes must also remain distinct.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Compare objectives, instruments, achievements and constraints by sector. Explain a linkage, such as agriculture supporting industrial demand, then evaluate uneven access and efficiency. A concise balanced answer is more useful than an unconnected chronology of every policy resolution.

topics.title: ESI glossary: retrieve a concept, then apply it

topics.summary: A small concept-use packet drawn from selected dictionary entries. All eight dictionary PDFs remain searchable in the catalogue; they are references, not eight books to memorise.

BoP: cross-border transaction record over a period
Crowding out: public activity may displace private spending

Opportunity cost: the forgone alternative

tables.title: Concept -> mechanism -> interpretation check

cells: BoP
Account of transactions between residents and the rest of the world.
Not only merchandise trade.
Crowding out
A possible reduction of private spending associated with public expansion.
State the financing and capacity context; do not claim every public project crowds out.
Externality
A positive or negative effect beyond the immediate transaction.
Private output value and social welfare effects can differ.
Opportunity cost
The alternative forgone by committing scarce resources.
It need not be a separate cash payment.
Fiscal drag
Progressive tax effects can restrain demand as incomes move into higher brackets.
Distinguish a built-in effect from a new discretionary tax decision.

cards.question: Original case: a government spends scarce funds on project A instead of feasible project B. What is the concept?
cards.answer: Opportunity cost: the forgone alternative use of resources. Explain the alternative, not just the money paid for A.

cards.question: Original case: factory output rises but neighbouring households face pollution. What should the GDP discussion include?
cards.answer: A negative external effect on welfare. Analyse output and social costs separately; do not assume higher production measures every welfare consequence.

cards.question: How should the dictionary be used during mock-test repair?
cards.answer: Identify the missed concept; retrieve its definition; create an original example and counterexample; retest in a fresh question. Do not replace applied study with alphabetical memorisation.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Economic vocabulary is useful only when it helps classify a real situation. For each term, learn the definition, the mechanism and a nearby concept it is not. This makes statement questions and descriptive answers more reliable than memorising isolated one-line labels.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone when scarce resources are committed. A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered. The opportunity cost of today's choice concerns what can still be done, not every past payment.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: An externality is an effect on others not fully reflected in the transaction's private cost or benefit. Pollution can make social cost exceed private cost; a beneficial spillover can make social benefit exceed private benefit. These gaps explain a case for carefully designed intervention, not an automatic justification for any intervention.

Crowding out describes a possible reduction in private spending associated with public expansion, for example through financing pressure. Crowding in describes public action making private activity more attractive, such as better infrastructure. Fiscal drag can arise when rising nominal incomes move taxpayers into higher effective burdens under an unchanged progressive structure.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative government chooses project A instead of feasible project B. The opportunity cost includes the benefit forgone from B; it is not merely the cash spent on A. If funds already wasted on an abandoned design are unrecoverable, they are sunk and do not alone justify spending more.

A factory's output rises while neighbours pay for treatment of polluted water. Production and private profit omit part of the social cost. The externality concept explains why growth and welfare assessments can diverge and why prevention or regulation may improve the outcome.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: BoP is broader than merchandise trade; inflation is broader than a single price; a fiscal deficit is a flow rather than a debt stock. Similar labels often hide different denominators, boundaries or time horizons.

Never infer a universal outcome from a possibility: public spending can crowd out, but need not always do so. State capacity, financing and implementation conditions. A textbook definition is not a current legal rule or threshold.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Use term -> example -> distinction -> implication. In a descriptive answer, include a concept only when it advances the reasoning. In an objective question, identify the tested boundary or denominator before searching memory for a familiar word.

topics.title: Growth and development: output, distribution and transformation

tables.title: Distinctions and policy tests

cells: Output vs welfare
Growth tracks production; development also tests how people live.
Pair output evidence with health, education, work and poverty outcomes.
Capital vs technology
More equipment expands inputs; innovation can raise output from given resources.
Ask whether investment is productive, not simply large.
Sectoral shift vs inclusion
Moving away from agriculture changes economic structure.
Judge whether workers gain productive opportunities rather than assuming every shift improves welfare.
Trickle-down vs deliberate inclusion
The traditional approach assumes output gains spread; the modern approach tests broader outcomes.
Explain the missing transmission channel when poverty persists.
Private gains vs social costs
Output may rise alongside pollution and resource loss.
Include environmental costs before calling a project developmental.

cells: World Bank / WDR 2026 (claimed)
AI gains require education, electricity, connectivity, affordable computing and accessible information; technology adoption alone is insufficient.
Illustrative India application: pair digital infrastructure with small-firm access, local-language tools and foundational learning to broaden productivity gains.
Examples such as UPI and IndiaAI in the compilation do not demonstrate measured causal effects. No return-on-investment estimate is supplied or inferred.

cells: UMANG
Electronics and IT / NeGD; unified access to Central/State government services.
Citizen service users; access to the application does not remove each underlying scheme's eligibility conditions.
Multi-platform service aggregation; the cited July 2021 map integration describes locating facilities, including Mera Ration fair-price-shop navigation.
